clue.text: Worthy Scotsman?

definitions.meaning: a worthy is a notable or celebrated person, someone on the top tier of the guest list
a man's given name common in Scotland, a variant spelling of Alistair

explanation.surface: A question about whether some respectable Scot deserves praise.
explanation.walkthrough: Read with the hyphen, the entry is A-LISTER, a top celebrity; without it, it is a Scottish first name. The question mark flags the name as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A worthy is a celebrated figure, the kind found on the top tier of fame; the name is a typical Scottish forename.

clue.text: Short term for Harvard, perhaps student's last one

parts.note: Harvard is an example of a university, shortened to uni

indicators.note: the final letter of the word student is taken, the possessive simply linking it

explanation.surface: A note on how a student might abbreviate their Ivy League university, and their final module.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last' picks T, the final letter of student (the apostrophe-s is grammar, not a letter to take).
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a single thing, the number one in counting or measurement.

clue.text: Diamonds pinched by, say, outwardly merry megastar?

indicators.note: the word for merry sits on the outside, wrapping the rest

parts.note: riant is a literary word for cheerful or laughing

indicators.note: diamonds is gripped inside the abbreviation for 'say'

parts.note: e.g. (for example) is what 'say' means here
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: A jolly celebrity, dripping in diamonds, gets robbed of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinched by' and 'outwardly' nest one piece in the next, making EDG and then the whole. Riant is a rare literary word. The question mark flags megastar taken literally: a huge star in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: A red giant is an enormous, cool, late-stage star, so literally a mega star rather than a celebrity.

clue.text: Corporal maybe about to undermine base again!

indicators.note: in a down entry, going under a piece means coming after it, so the rest is placed below the base

parts.note: e is the base of natural logarithms in mathematics
a corporal is a non-commissioned officer, NCO
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A corporal on the point of sabotaging the army base once more.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'to undermine' puts NCO and RE beneath E. Encore is the cry for a repeat performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Encore is the audience's call for a repeat, so an exclamation meaning 'once more!'

clue.text: Prone to change input to notable support for wine producers

indicators.note: the rearranged letters are fed into the middle of the notable

parts.note: a notable is a VIP, a very important person

indicators.note: the letters of the word prone are altered in order

explanation.surface: Something inclined to alter what a celebrity contributes to a winery's backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to change' gives NEPRO, which 'input to' places in the middle of the notable. 'Wine producers' are the vines themselves, not vintners.
explanation.definitionFit: A vine-prop is a stake holding up grapevines, the plants that yield the fruit for wine.

clue.text: 45 degrees required to get brown in a month

indicators.note: the colour word goes inside the month

parts.note: Oct is the short form of October
tan is a light brown

explanation.surface: How many degrees of heat it takes to get a suntan within a month.
explanation.definitionFit: An octant is an eighth of a circle, an arc or sector spanning that angle.

clue.text: Check incision around opening in pericardium

indicators.note: the word for incision wraps round the picked letter

parts.note: insection is a rare word for a cut made into something

indicators.note: the first letter of pericardium is its opening

explanation.surface: A surgeon checks a cut made around the opening in the heart's membrane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts P inside INSECTION after its S. The surgical surface pushes towards SECTION, but the rarer INSECTION is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: An inspection is a careful examination, the noun sense of a check.

clue.text: Perhaps slip on ice when twisting drill

parts.note: re means on, in the sense of concerning

indicators.note: the word ice is turned about into a new order

parts.note: PT, physical training, is exercise drill

explanation.surface: Someone loses their footing on ice while turning a power drill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twisting' turns ICE into CEI. 'Slip' here is a paper slip, not a fall.
explanation.definitionFit: A receipt is one example of a slip, a small piece of paper recording a purchase.

clue.text: After November, around noon, getting light

indicators.note: the time word wraps round the letter for noon

parts.note: later means after in time
N is November in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: After November, around midday, it brightens up.
explanation.walkthrough: LATER goes around N to make LANTER, and then another N follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A lantern is a portable lamp, so a source of light.

clue.text: Enrage because of commentator's opinion

parts.note: in can mean because of, as in 'in view of'

indicators.note: a commentator speaks, so the word is given as it is heard

parts.note: sense can mean an opinion, as in 'the sense of the meeting'

explanation.surface: A pundit's view is enough to make someone furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commentator's' signals that SENSE is heard, then spelt CENSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To incense someone is to make them very angry, a synonym of enrage.

clue.text: Principal introducing thorough test about English to inspire others?

indicators.note: the test is brought into the middle of that word
the word for principal goes around the letter for English

parts.note: staple means chief or principal, as in a staple diet
a good exam is a searching, thorough test

explanation.surface: A head teacher brings in a rigorous English exam to motivate the others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts E inside STAPLE (SETAPLE); 'introducing' then puts GOODEXAM inside that, after SETA. 'Principal' looks like the school head but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting a good example means behaving so as to encourage others to follow; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Include up-front ethnic minority couple

indicators.note: the front letters of the words ethnic and minority are taken

parts.note: a brace is a pair, as in a brace of pheasants

explanation.surface: A call for an ethnic minority couple to be welcomed openly.
explanation.definitionFit: To embrace something is to take it in or encompass it, a synonym of include.

clue.text: Excellent supporter very independent old spinster rejected

parts.note: a bra is a supporting undergarment

indicators.note: turned back, so these letters are read in reverse

parts.note: an unmarried woman is addressed as Miss

explanation.surface: An admirer praises a very self-reliant old maid who was turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' reverses O+MISS to SSIMO. Bravissimo is Italian, the superlative of bravo, used as a cry of applause.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravissimo is an exclamation of the highest praise, meaning 'superb!'

clue.text: Better to follow speed limit, sort of

indicators.note: the word for better comes after the word for speed

parts.note: rate means speed, as in a rate of knots
to cap something is to better or outdo it

explanation.surface: Advice that it is better to obey the speed limit, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a rate-cap was a government limit on how much a local council could raise in rates, its property tax.
explanation.definitionFit: A rate-cap is a ceiling imposed on charges or local taxes, one particular kind of restriction.

clue.text: In which Old Bill might stop between stages of a cycling tour?

definitions.text: In which Old Bill might stop between stages of a cycling tour?

parts.words: In which Old Bill might stop between stages of a cycling tour?
parts.note: an old paper bill is thrown away and later recycled; the 'cycling tour' is its trip round the recycling loop, and Old Bill is British slang for the police

explanation.surface: The police take a rest stop during a bike race like the Tour de France.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Bill is British slang for the police, which suggests a cycling-race scene. Read literally, an old bill (an invoice) rests in the bin before it is recycled.
explanation.definitionFit: A container for discarded paper, where a used invoice lands before going off for recycling.

clue.text: Demonstrator collecting papers for supplier

indicators.note: the word for demonstrator gathers the papers inside it

parts.note: a prover is one who demonstrates or proves something
ID, identity documents, are one's papers

explanation.surface: A protester picks up some documents on behalf of a vendor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demonstrator' suggests a protester; here it is one who proves.
explanation.definitionFit: A provider is one who furnishes goods or services, a synonym of supplier.

clue.text: Creature's face bitten by climbing snake

definitions.note: the apostrophe-s stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: the face is held within the jaws of the reversed snake
in a down entry, climbing means reading upwards, so the snake is reversed

parts.note: an adder is a venomous snake
pan is slang for a face

explanation.surface: An animal gets bitten on the face by a snake that is climbing a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbing' makes REDDA, and 'bitten by' sets the face inside those jaws. The 's of Creature's is 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A red panda is a small reddish tree-dwelling mammal of the Himalayas, an example of an animal.

clue.text: Fictional character giving and receiving pain, extremely authoritarian

parts.note: S and M, sadism and masochism, is the giving and taking of pain

indicators.note: the outer letters of authoritarian are taken

explanation.surface: A storybook figure who dishes out and takes pain, and is very bossy.
explanation.walkthrough: S and M is shorthand for sadomasochism.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sandman is a figure of folklore who sprinkles sand to bring sleep to children.

clue.text: By 2 am, second terrible natural disaster

indicators.note: these letters are put into a dreadful jumble

parts.note: the answer to 2 down, a word meaning one

explanation.surface: Something awful strikes just before two in the morning, a second disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: '2' borrows the answer to 2 down, UNIT; with AM and S, 'terrible' shuffles UNITAMS.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsunami is a huge sea wave caused by an earthquake, a classic catastrophe of nature.

clue.text: Mentioned in question report of involuntary escape from trap?

definitions.text: report of involuntary escape from trap?

indicators.note: said out loud, so the phrase is given by how it sounds

parts.note: a matter in question is one at issue

explanation.surface: Something brought up during questioning about a report of a prisoner's escape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mentioned' says AT ISSUE is heard. 'Trap' is slang for the mouth, and the involuntary escape is a sneeze.
explanation.definitionFit: Atishoo is the British imitative word for the noise of a sneeze, a burst of air from the mouth.

clue.text: That girl getting on with German in solitary

parts.note: her refers to a girl already mentioned
mit is the German word for with

explanation.surface: A girl making progress with a German speaker while in solitary confinement.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermit is a recluse; 'a solitary' is a noun for one who lives alone.

clue.text: Setter runs out of foreign currency leaving quarters for natives

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as me

indicators.note: the letter for runs is taken out of the currency

parts.note: the dinar is a currency used in several Arab and Balkan countries
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: The puzzle-setter runs out of foreign cash, leaving lodgings for local people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' removes R from DINARS, leaving DINAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A medina is the old walled Arab quarter of a North African town, as opposed to colonial districts.

clue.text: What may go after cheese, overshadowing small dessert

indicators.note: the rodent sits over and around the small letter

parts.note: a mouse chases cheese, as in a mousetrap

explanation.surface: Talk of what follows the cheese course, dwarfing a tiny pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What may go after cheese' suggests the next course of a meal, but it is the rodent that chases it.
explanation.definitionFit: A mousse is a light, airy sweet dish set with whipped cream or egg whites.

clue.text: Elbow may split due to this affront prior to talking

definitions.text: Elbow may split due to this

indicators.note: the insult comes before the word for talking

parts.note: to dis someone is slang for insulting them
articulation is clear speech

explanation.surface: A slight before a conversation makes someone storm off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elbow' looks like a verb (to elbow someone aside) but is the joint, which comes apart at its articulation.
explanation.definitionFit: Disarticulation is separation at a joint, the way an elbow may come apart.

clue.text: Second in race, in a short distance, becomes leader

parts.note: a means one, written as the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: the picked letter goes inside the following letters

parts.note: mm, millimetres, is a tiny length

indicators.note: the second letter of race is picked

explanation.surface: Coming second in a race by a whisker turns into a win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second in' gives A from race; 'in' puts it inside I and MM.
explanation.definitionFit: An imam is a Muslim prayer leader, or a spiritual head of a community.

clue.text: Branch officers initially anger cabinet

parts.note: an arm is a branch, of a tree or an organisation

indicators.note: the opening letter of officers is taken

parts.note: ire means anger

explanation.surface: Local branch officers stir up resentment in the government cabinet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cabinet' looks political, but it is the furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: An armoire is a tall, ornate wardrobe or cupboard, a kind of cabinet.

clue.text: Piece of plan to stop missus coming back

indicators.note: the plan plugs the gap in the middle of the reversed title
the title is turned round to run backwards

parts.note: Mrs is the title spoken as missus
an idea is a plan

explanation.surface: Part of a scheme to keep one's wife from returning home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming back' makes SRM, and 'to stop' plugs the plan into it. 'Piece' looks like a part of the plan but is gangster slang for a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidearm is a pistol worn at the side, and a piece is underworld slang for a handgun.
